Metadata.description: Instant interpretation of medical lab tests using AI

Hero.title: ABOUT THE PROJECT
Hero.description: WebDoc.life is a free, intelligent AI service for interpreting medical test results. Advanced recognition algorithms instantly read data from your photos or PDF documents. Get a structured, detailed, and easy-to-understand breakdown of your lab results in seconds - without the queues or complex medical reference books.

feature1.content: It reviews your lab results and identifies risk zones, saving you both time and money.

feature2.title: EXPLAINS POTENTIAL CAUSES:

items.question: How does the test interpretation work?
items.answer: We send the image of your PDF file or photo to a vision model that reads the values itself, then pass the result to a medical AI. The system compares the data with generally accepted reference values and helps structure the information.

items.question: Is it safe? Do you store my data?
items.answer: Security is our priority. Before processing, we remove personal information (name, contacts) from the documents. All uploaded files are stored in an encrypted format, and you can completely delete them from your profile at any time.

items.question: Does this replace a visit to the doctor?
items.answer: Not at all. WebDoc.life provides reference information for self-education and preparation for a consultation. To get a diagnosis, prescribe treatment, or interpret complex pathologies, you must consult a qualified doctor.

items.question: What types of tests and formats are supported?
items.answer: The service works best with general and biochemical blood and urine tests, as well as hormone tests. You can upload files in PDF, JPG, and PNG formats. The main thing is that the text on the image is clear and readable.

items.question: How much does it cost to use the service?
items.answer: At the current stage, WebDoc.life is a completely free project. Our goal is to make complex medical information accessible to everyone, helping people better understand their body's metrics.

About.title: About webdoc.life Technology
About.description: This project was created as a demonstration of modern AI capabilities in medicine. We hand the report image to a vision model to turn complex laboratory forms into clear, understandable reports.

mockData.generalComment: ATTENTION: Significant deviations in carbohydrate and lipid metabolism parameters, as well as moderate signs of liver damage (probably fatty hepatosis), have been detected. The condition is not critical, but requires a routine medical consultation to adjust lifestyle and prescribe supportive therapy.
mockData.reasoning: An elevated fasting glucose level (6.8 mmol/L) indicates impaired carbohydrate tolerance (prediabetes) or the development of type 2 diabetes. Against this background, pronounced dyslipidemia (elevated LDL cholesterol) and a moderate increase in liver enzymes (ALT, AST) are observed, which is a classic picture of metabolic syndrome and non-alcoholic fatty liver disease. C-reactive protein (12 mg/L) reflects the presence of low-grade systemic inflammation associated with excess weight or a metabolic disorder.

causes.title: Insulin Resistance / Prediabetes
causes.description: Decreased sensitivity of body cells to insulin, which causes glucose to not be absorbed properly and accumulate in the blood.

causes.title: Fatty Hepatosis (Hepatic Steatosis)
causes.description: Accumulation of excess fat in liver cells, leading to their slow destruction and release of ALT and AST into the blood.

causes.title: Dyslipidemia
causes.description: Lipid metabolism disorder with a predominance of 'bad' cholesterol (LDL), which increases the risk of atherosclerotic plaques.

recommendations.text: Schedule a routine consultation with a general practitioner and endocrinologist to assess the risks of type 2 diabetes.
An abdominal ultrasound is recommended to confirm fatty hepatosis, as well as a glycated hemoglobin (HbA1c) test.
Strict diet correction: minimize simple carbohydrates (sugar, baked goods), add fiber and healthy fats to the diet.
Gradual introduction of regular physical activity (walking, swimming) to increase tissue sensitivity to insulin and reduce weight.
